content: At the start of the program, over 40 million individuals were incapacitated and disfigured due to lymphatic filariasis (LF)-related diseases, primarily lymphedema and its advanced form, elephantiasis, as well as hydrocele. The program has two primary objectives: first, to halt the transmission of LF infections through mass drug administration (MDA), and second, to alleviate suffering by managing morbidity and preventing disability (MMDP). To date, 7 billion doses of medication have been distributed to more than 910 million people at least once. Interventions under the Global Programme to Eliminate Lymphatic Filariasis (GPELF) are estimated to have prevented over 97 million cases of LF. However, efforts to prevent and manage LF-related disabilities in endemic communities remain limited. Among the 72 endemic countries, only 60 have reported limited data on LF morbidity, and only 5% of implementation units with known LF patients are providing MMDP care. The GPELF strategy is built on two pillars: interrupting LF transmission and alleviating the suffering of those affected by the disease. Vector control, when appropriately implemented, can complement activities aimed at halting transmission. By 2018, only 37 countries were reporting MMDP activities at the implementation unit level, indicating active efforts in morbidity management and disability prevention. The GPELF strategic plan mandates that by 2021, all endemic countries should collect and report MMDP data to the World Health Organization (WHO). Despite global expansion of MMDP services, a rapid scale-up is necessary to meet the 2030 targets. This document provides guidance for national programs on planning, implementing, and monitoring MMDP activities in alignment with the GPELF essential care package for LF. It summarizes the best available information on managing morbidity and preventing disability associated with acute attacks, lymphedema, and hydrocele. Additionally, it offers operational and managerial guidance to reduce LF cases and provide care for affected individuals. The target audience for this document includes managers of national LF programs, public health officials, and medical or non-medical staff responsible for designing, implementing, and sustaining LF-related activities. It also emphasizes integrating LF activities with other health initiatives. The document is organized into sections: background information on GPELF and LF-associated morbidity, strategies for MMDP, and guidance for building national MMDP programs tailored to local contexts. Annexes provide tools and resources for use in hospitals, health facilities, and communities. Lymphatic filariasis is a vector-borne infection caused by three species of thread-like parasitic worms, with Wuchereria bancrofti being the most prevalent worldwide. The adult worms reside in the lymphatic system, with a reproductive lifespan of 4–6 years, producing millions of microfilariae that circulate in the blood. These are transmitted between humans by various mosquito species. Before widespread control efforts, an estimated 120 million people globally were infected with LF, with 856 million people still living in areas requiring MDA as of 2018. Over 80% of those affected reside in India and endemic African countries, with the remainder in Southeast Asia, the Eastern Mediterranean, and the Pacific. Approximately 17 million people globally suffer from LF-related lymphedema (or elephantiasis), characterized by swelling of the limbs, breasts, or genitals. Nearly 19 million men are affected by urogenital swelling, primarily hydrocele. While these conditions are rarely fatal, they rank LF as one of the leading causes of permanent and long-term disability worldwide. LF infection can occur early in life, with about 30% of children in some areas infected before the age of 4. Although clinical disease typically manifests later, subclinical damage begins early. LF is unlikely to cause lymphedema or hydrocele in children under 10–15 years of age. The acute form of LF, known as adenolymphangitis (ADL), includes acute dermatolymphangioadenitis (ADLA) and acute filarial lymphangitis (AFL). ADLA, often referred to as acute attacks, involves inflammation of the skin, lymph vessels, and glands due to secondary bacterial infection and requires antibiotic therapy. AFL, caused by the death of adult worms, is generally self-limiting. Chronic manifestations include lymphedema, hydrocele, chyluria, and tropical pulmonary eosinophilia (TPE). Lymphedema, particularly in its advanced form of elephantiasis, primarily affects the lower limbs and is more common in women. It can also involve the arms, breasts, or genitals. Hydrocele, resulting from fluid accumulation in the scrotal cavity, typically presents as painless scrotal swelling in post-pubertal males. Other clinical manifestations include chyluria, characterized by milky urine due to ruptured lymphatic vessels, and TPE, a syndrome caused by immunologic hyperresponsiveness to microfilariae in the lungs. TPE is marked by cough, fever, eosinophilia, elevated serum immunoglobulin E, and positive antifilarial antibodies. LF imposes a significant socioeconomic burden. Lymphedema and hydrocele lead to permanent disability, disfigurement, and psychosocial consequences. Direct economic costs for managing acute and chronic manifestations are substantial, with patients often bearing the financial burden. Indirect losses due to reduced productivity further strain local and national economies. Chronic complications, often stigmatized, prevent patients from participating fully in society and leading fulfilling lives. For men, genital damage causes physical limitations and social stigma, while women with lymphedema or elephantiasis face severe stigmatization, often making marriage and social integration impossible. These challenges can lead to depression and poor mental health, affecting not only patients but also their families, especially if the patient is the primary income earner. The WHO International Classification of Functioning, Disability, and Health provides a framework for understanding the biological, individual, and social dimensions of health in LF patients. Disability in LF is defined as impairments, activity limitations, and participation restrictions caused by the disease. These disabilities can be mitigated by addressing environmental and personal factors.
